findings.claim: The LCEN site-identification duty is no longer "article 6-III" — since 23 May 2024 it sits in article 1-1 of loi n° 2004-575, and article 6 now covers intermediaries only.
findings.detail: The consolidated LCEN page on Légifrance prints the éditeur identification obligation under the heading Article 1-1, marked "Version en vigueur depuis le 23/05/2024" (the loi SREN n° 2024-449 of 21 May 2024 restructured the LCEN). The substance is unchanged; only the citation is stale. Any mentions légales page or memo citing "art. 6-III LCEN" should now cite art. 1-1.
findings.source_quote: Les personnes dont l'activité est d'éditer un service de communication au public en ligne mettent à la disposition du public, dans un standard ouvert : 1° S'il s'agit de personnes physiques, leurs nom, prénoms, domicile et numéro de téléphone... — heading "Article 1-1", "Version en vigueur depuis le 23/05/2024"

findings.claim: (a) The non-professional publisher's anonymity regime survived the renumbering intact: Gabriel may publish only GitHub's name and address, not his own, provided he has given GitHub his identity.
findings.detail: This governs the SITE (copius.fr), not the newsletter message. Two conditions: he must edit "à titre non professionnel" (true today — nothing for sale), and his identification details must be held by the hosting provider (GitHub holds his account identity). The hébergeur is bound to professional secrecy on those details except before a judicial authority. The moment he sells, he is no longer non-professional and this paragraph stops protecting him.
findings.source_quote: Les personnes éditant à titre non professionnel un service de communication au public en ligne peuvent ne tenir à la disposition du public, pour préserver leur anonymat, que le nom, la dénomination ou la raison sociale et l'adresse du fournisseur de services d'hébergement, sous réserve d'avoir communiqué à ce fournisseur les éléments d'identification personnelle mentionnés au I du présent article.

findings.claim: (a) The CPCE prospection régime does not bite today: "prospection directe" is defined as promoting goods, services, or the image of a person who SELLS goods or provides services. Gabriel sells nothing, so article L34-5's opt-in rule is not triggered by a free editorial letter.
findings.detail: This is the pivot of the whole answer. L34-5 transposes the e-privacy consent rule, and its own definition is commercial by construction. A free bilingual culinary atlas newsletter from someone with nothing for sale promotes no seller's goods, services, or image. The GDPR still applies in full (see below) — what falls away is the specific L34-5 prior-consent obligation and its message-content duties.
findings.source_quote: Constitue une prospection directe l'envoi de tout message destiné à promouvoir, directement ou indirectement, des biens, des services ou l'image d'une personne vendant des biens ou fournissant des services.

findings.claim: (a,b) Even where L34-5 DOES apply, it requires "coordonnées valables" for opting out and a non-concealed sender identity — it never says "adresse postale".
findings.detail: The full paragraph names two prohibitions: sending without valid contact details through which the recipient can effectively ask that the messages stop free of charge, and concealing the identity of the person on whose behalf the message is sent (plus no misleading subject line). A working unsubscribe link and a real reply-to address (contact@copius.fr) satisfy "coordonnées valables". Version en vigueur depuis le 26 juillet 2020.
findings.source_quote: Dans tous les cas, il est interdit d'émettre, à des fins de prospection directe, des messages au moyen de système automatisé de communications électroniques au sens du 6° de l'article L. 32, télécopieurs et courriers électroniques, sans indiquer de coordonnées valables auxquelles le destinataire puisse utilement transmettre une demande tendant à obtenir que ces communications cessent sans frais autres que ceux liés à la transmission de celle-ci. Il est également interdit de dissimuler l'identité de la personne pour le compte de laquelle la communication est émise et de mentionner un objet sans rapport avec la prestation ou le service proposé.

findings.claim: (a,b) CNIL's own rule for NON-commercial prospection is opt-out, not opt-in: inform the person and let them object simply and free of charge.
findings.detail: CNIL's prospection page carves out non-commercial prospection (its example is caritative) and attaches two conditions only — being informed that the address will be used for non-commercial prospection, and being able to object simply and free of charge. Gabriel should still take a real opt-in, because that is the cleanest GDPR consent and the cleanest proof, but he is not standing on the stricter commercial régime.
findings.source_quote: Si la prospection n'est pas de nature commerciale (exemple : caritative) — la personne doit « être informée » que son adresse électronique ou son numéro de téléphone sera utilisé à des fins de prospection « non commerciale » et « être en mesure de s'opposer » à cette utilisation de manière simple et gratuite

findings.claim: (b) What CNIL actually requires INSIDE the message is two things: the sender's identity, and a simple way to refuse. Nothing else.
findings.detail: CNIL states it as one sentence covering every solicitation. "Identité de l'organisation qui l'émet" is satisfied by "Copius — copius.fr" plus a real reply address; it does not require a legal name plus domicile in the message. "Un moyen simple" is the unsubscribe link.
findings.source_quote: chaque sollicitation doit obligatoirement permettre à la personne concernée de prendre connaissance de l'identité de l'organisation qui l'émet ainsi que d'exprimer, si elle le souhaite et par un moyen simple, son refus

findings.claim: (b) No French text I opened requires a postal address inside a newsletter message. I checked all four candidate homes and none contains one.
findings.detail: Checked: CPCE L34-5 (says "coordonnées valables", never "adresse"); CNIL's two prospection pages (no occurrence of "adresse postale" — CNIL treats postal prospection on a separate page); CNIL's "règles d'or", which places the controller's contact details on the UNSUBSCRIBE PAGE, not in the message, and says "coordonnées" not "adresse postale"; LCEN art. 1-1, which governs the site's mentions légales, not message content. This is a negative claim from four opened primary sources, not from absence of search hits.
findings.source_quote: Indiquez sur la page de désinscription le nom et les coordonnées du responsable du traitement et du propriétaire du fichier source s'il est différent du responsable du traitement.

findings.claim: The postal-address demand he hit is a US CAN-SPAM rule, not a French one: the FTC requires a valid physical postal address in every commercial email.
findings.detail: US-facing ESPs build this into onboarding and footers for all customers regardless of jurisdiction. That explains the Brevo wall without any French law standing behind it. The FTC rule attaches to messages whose primary purpose is commercial advertisement or promotion of a product or service — which a free editorial letter is not, but the platform does not adjudicate that per account.
findings.source_quote: Your message must include your valid physical postal address.

findings.claim: (c) Selling flips three separate switches at once, and the first is the one he will not see coming: his home address becomes publishable.
findings.detail: (1) LCEN art. 1-1 — he stops being "à titre non professionnel", so nom, prénoms, domicile and numéro de téléphone go into the mentions légales, plus the hébergeur's details. (2) CPCE L34-5 — the newsletter now promotes "l'image d'une personne vendant des biens", so prior express consent becomes mandatory for every B2C address, and every message needs coordonnées valables and an undisguised sender. (3) LCEN art. 19 — as a distance seller he owes "un accès facile, direct et permanent" to name, the address where he is established, email, telephone, and registry number. A domiciliation address, not his flat, is the answer to all three; this is the legal reason the domiciliation is the real blocker, not the newsletter.
findings.source_quote: Toute personne qui exerce l'activité définie à l'article 14 est tenue d'assurer à ceux à qui est destinée la fourniture de biens ou la prestation de services un accès facile, direct et permanent utilisant un standard ouvert aux informations suivantes

findings.claim: (d) The right RGPD basis is consent, article 6(1)(a) — and he must be able to demonstrate it, with withdrawal as easy as giving it.
findings.detail: Legitimate interest 6(1)(f) is arguable for a free editorial letter, but consent matches the act the reader actually performs (typing an address into a subscribe box) and is what CNIL's opt-in guidance describes. Article 7(1) puts the burden of proof on him; article 7(3) requires withdrawal to be as simple as consent. Note CNIL's own newsletter runs on 6(1)(e), mission d'intérêt public — a basis unavailable to a private individual, so do not copy CNIL's notice wording.
findings.source_quote: Article 7(1) : le responsable doit pouvoir « démontrer que la personne concernée a donné son consentement » ; Article 7(3) : « Il est aussi simple de retirer que de donner son consentement »

findings.claim: (d) The privacy notice must carry nine items, and his current page — "no form, no mailing list, no analytics" — becomes false the day a subscribe box ships.
findings.detail: CNIL's required mentions: identity and contact details of the controller; purposes; legal basis; whether providing the data is obligatory or optional; recipients or categories of recipients (this is where the email platform goes, as a sous-traitant); retention period; data subject rights; DPO contact details where one exists (he has none — say so rather than omitting the line); and the right to lodge a complaint with the CNIL. Delivery must be concise, transparent, comprehensible and easily accessible, at the point of collection, with a link to the full notice.
findings.source_quote: Identité et coordonnées de l'organisme (responsable du traitement de données) ; Finalités ; Base légale du traitement de données ; Caractère obligatoire ou facultatif du recueil des données ; Destinataires ou catégories de destinataires des données ; Durée de conservation des données ; Droits des personnes concernées ; Coordonnées du délégué à la protection des données ; Droit d'introduire une réclamation auprès de la CNIL

findings.claim: (d) Yes, he needs a registre des traitements — the small-entity exemption does not cover a standing mailing list, because that processing is not occasional.
findings.detail: CNIL states the obligation covers every organisme whatever its size, and that sub-250-employee entities must still register non-occasional processing, risky processing, and sensitive data. A permanent subscriber list is non-occasional by definition. The household exemption in art. 2(2)(c) does not rescue him either: a newsletter published to the public is not a "activité strictement personnelle ou domestique", and art. 4(7) makes any natural person who determines purposes and means a responsable du traitement. In practice this is one page: purpose, basis, data (email, subscription date), recipients (the ESP), retention, security. Not a burden — but not optional.
findings.source_quote: L'obligation de tenir un registre des traitements concerne tous les organismes, publics comme privés et quelle que soit leur taille. […] les traitements non occasionnels

findings.claim: (e) Double opt-in is not legally required in France. No text imposes it, and none of the CNIL pages I opened uses the term.
findings.detail: What the law requires is a consent that is libre, spécifique, éclairé et univoque — a dedicated, non-pre-ticked checkbox or an explicit subscribe action — plus the ability to prove it under art. 7(1). Double opt-in is the cheapest way to discharge that burden and it also blocks someone from subscribing a third party's address, which matters for a static site with no account system. Recommend it on evidentiary grounds, not as a legal obligation. I could not open a CNIL page that names double opt-in either way; sources asserting "la CNIL recommande fortement le double opt-in" were commentary sites, which I did not treat as sources.
findings.source_quote: Le consentement doit être libre, spécifique, éclairé et univoque. Il requiert, pour être valable, une action positive et spécifique de la personne concernée (exemple : une case à cocher dédiée et qui ne soit pas pré-cochée).

findings.claim: CNIL's opt-in/opt-out explainer independently confirms the non-commercial carve-out by listing "prospection caritative" on the opt-out side.
findings.detail: A second CNIL page reaching the same conclusion as the prospection page, through different wording. Useful corroboration for the load-bearing claim that the opt-in régime is commercial-only.
findings.source_quote: L'opt-out s'applique notamment à la publicité postale, aux communications électroniques pour des produits similaires à ceux déjà achetés, à la prospection B2B, et à la prospection caritative.

unknowns: Whether Brevo's onboarding postal address is contractually mandatory or merely a default footer field. I searched Brevo's help centre and found pages on the unsubscribe link but none stating a postal-address requirement; I did not open an authenticated onboarding screen. His first-hand account of the wall stands as the record; the legal cause is CAN-SPAM-shaped, but I did not verify Brevo's own wording.

Which email platforms accept a French account with no postal address. Not researched here — that is a lane-2 question, and any answer must be dated and quoted from the provider's own terms, never from memory.

The exact sanction for missing mentions légales under the post-SREN LCEN. Search summaries quoted 1 year / 75,000 EUR for a natural person, but I did not open the penal provision in the renumbered law, so I am not asserting it.

Whether a free newsletter could ever be recharacterised as promoting "l'image d'une personne vendant des biens" during the run-up to a June 2027 launch — for instance a letter that pre-announces a paid product. The definition turns on the message's promotional object, and a waitlist or launch teaser is where the line gets tested. Worth re-checking before any pre-launch campaign.
Whether CNIL has ever taken a position on double opt-in in a published deliberation or referentiel. My negative is bounded by the pages I opened, not by a full survey of CNIL's sanctions corpus.
research.bottom_line: Yes, he can run the newsletter now, and French law does not require his home address anywhere in it. Three separate régimes get conflated and they resolve differently for him. (1) The site's mentions légales: the duty is no longer article 6-III — since 23 May 2024 the loi SREN moved it to article 1-1 of the LCEN, and the non-professional anonymity paragraph survived intact, so he may publish GitHub's name and address instead of his own, provided GitHub holds his identity, which it does. (2) The prospection régime: CPCE L34-5 defines prospection directe as promoting goods, services or the image of a person who SELLS — he sells nothing, so the opt-in rule is not triggered, and CNIL's own page puts non-commercial prospection under an inform-and-let-them-object régime. (3) Inside the message, CNIL requires exactly two things: the sender's identity and a simple way to refuse. I checked all four places a postal-address rule could live — L34-5, both CNIL prospection pages, LCEN art. 1-1 — and none contains one; the requirement he hit at Brevo is the US CAN-SPAM rule, "Your message must include your valid physical postal address", which US-facing platforms apply to every account regardless of jurisdiction. So the blocker was the platform, not the law. What he does owe: a real opt-in (non-pre-ticked, one clear action), a working unsubscribe in every message, a rewritten privacy page carrying CNIL's nine mentions — his current "no form, no mailing list" text becomes false the day a subscribe box ships — consent under art. 6(1)(a) that he can prove under art. 7(1), and a one-page registre des traitements, which the sub-250 exemption does not waive because a standing list is non-occasional processing. Double opt-in is not legally required; recommend it as the cheapest proof of consent and as protection against someone subscribing a third party's address. The moment he sells, all three régimes flip together — his nom, prénoms, domicile and téléphone become publishable under art. 1-1, prior consent becomes mandatory under L34-5, and art. 19 adds the e-commerce disclosure duty. That is the legal reason the domiciliation address is the real prerequisite for June 2027, and why it is a separate problem from the newsletter, which he can start without it.

research.lane: LANE 2 — THE ADDRESS PROBLEM (domiciliation, association, boîte postale, INSEE/INPI publication rules)

findings.claim: (a) A domiciliation commerciale is an administrative/legal address supplied by an approved business centre; having an address is compulsory for any registered business.
findings.detail: Service-Public (société page, 'Vérifié le 15 septembre 2025') defines it and adds that the provider needs a prefectural licence and that the contract runs 3 months minimum. The same site's individual-business page ('Vérifié le 02 juillet 2026') repeats the obligation for an EI or micro-entreprise. What it provides is an address, mail receipt/forwarding and, in the paid tiers, meeting rooms or secretarial services — not premises you occupy.
findings.source_quote: La domiciliation d'une société est obligatoire. Il s'agit de lui donner une adresse administrative. […] Un cabinet (ou société) de domiciliation est un centre d'affaires dont l'activité est de fournir une adresse à des entreprises. Il doit posséder un agrément préfectoral.

findings.claim: (a) SeDomicilier, article dated 8 July 2026: 20 €/month HT with no commitment (16 € promo), down to 14 €/month HT on a 3-year commitment (11 € promo).
findings.detail: Vendor-published price list, dated on the page itself. The article also states the price does not depend on the legal form: 'le tarif de domiciliation ne dépend pas de la forme juridique (SASU, EURL, SARL, micro-entreprise, SCI)'. All figures excl. VAT; mail forwarding and scanning are usually priced on top.
findings.source_quote: de 11€ à 16€/mois

findings.claim: (a) LegalPlace, guide 'Dernière mise à jour le 18/05/2026': 17 € HT/month for a micro-entreprise or SCI, 25 € HT/month for a SARL/EURL/SAS/SASU, address in Paris 2e.
findings.detail: Second named provider with its own dated price. Its market range for a plain address is given as 10–70 €/month depending on city and services — treat that range as vendor editorial, not a measured market survey.
findings.source_quote: Les tarifs de domiciliation commerciale chez LegalPlace démarrent à 17 € HT / mois pour une micro-entreprise ou une SCI, et à 25 € HT / mois pour une SARL, une EURL, une SAS ou une SASU.

findings.claim: (a) Third named provider, Kandbaz: association address advertised at under 20 €/month, with a 1 €/month 3-month promo.
findings.detail: Page carries no visible date, so the figure is dated only by the fetch (15 Sept 2026). Useful mainly because it is an association-specific offer.
findings.source_quote: une adresse prestigieuse pour moins de 20 €/mois

findings.claim: (b) No. A commercial domiciliation contract is sold to a business — existing or in the course of registration — not to a private individual with no entity and no project.
findings.detail: Three converging opened sources: Service-Public defines the domiciliataire's activity as supplying an address 'à des entreprises'; the AML rules make the domiciliataire identify 'le client (entreprise)' and its beneficial owner before signing (Kandbaz LCB-FT page, 19 November 2025); and the domiciliation contract's function is to be the justificatif de jouissance filed at the INPI guichet unique. No opened source states an outright legal ban on selling to a person with no entity, so this is 'that is not what the product is', not 'it is forbidden'.
findings.source_quote: identifier le client (entreprise) et, le cas échéant, le bénéficiaire effectif

findings.claim: (b) You can sign before the entity exists: the attestation/contrat de domiciliation is what lets you register, and it may carry the mention 'en cours d'immatriculation' instead of a SIREN.
findings.detail: LegalPlace guide, 'last updated 13/04/2026'. Practical consequence for Gabriel: the sequence is decide to create the entity → take the address → register with it, not the reverse. He cannot buy the address first and decide later.
findings.source_quote: en cours d'immatriculation

findings.claim: (b) What a private individual can buy instead is a mail box (domiciliation postale). It is explicitly not a proof of residence and is not a personal address.
findings.detail: SeDomicilier's own article for individuals (written 27 Oct 2017, last updated 12 Aug 2025) sells the service to individuals but disclaims its legal value. An older provider blog (abcliv, 05/07/2017) states flatly: 'Il est formellement interdit d'utiliser une adresse postale comme justificatif de domicile.' Whether such a box may be printed as a contact address in a newsletter footer is a contractual question for the provider's CGV, not settled by these pages.
findings.source_quote: it is impossible to use the address of your domiciliation box as proof of residence

findings.claim: (c) Alternative — attestation d'hébergement from a third party (school, employer, parent). Mechanically possible: a host signs an attestation authorising the business address at their premises.
findings.detail: LegalPlace, 13/04/2026, describes the hébergeant route alongside owner and domiciliation-company routes. Service-Public's EI page lists the matching proof: a housing attestation plus a proof of address in the host's name, less than 3 months old. In practice a public lycée hosting a student's business or association siège would need its own decision — no source found either way, so treat a school address as unverified, not as an option on the table.
findings.source_quote: A third party providing free accommodation must sign an attestation d'hébergement (hosting attestation) authorizing the business domiciliation at their address.

findings.claim: (c) Alternative — La Poste boîte postale (Flexigo). Rentable by individuals, annual or seasonal, but you must prove a home address to get one, and the page publishes no price.
findings.detail: La Poste's own page: individuals must present 'une pièce d'identité valide et justifier de votre domicile'. Annual subscriptions renew automatically each January; seasonal rental bills any started month, one month minimum. No 2026 tariff appears on that page and the 2026 tariff PDFs I searched did not surface a BP line. Note also that a BP is refused as an association's siège: Kandbaz states the address 'ne doit pas correspondre à une simple boîte postale'.
findings.source_quote: Une boîte postale constitue un espace de stockage personnel situé dans un bureau de Poste.

findings.claim: (c) Alternative — coworking space or pépinière d'entreprises, listed by Service-Public as valid domiciliation for an EI/micro-entreprise.
findings.detail: Same EI page, verified 2 July 2026. A pépinière is limited to businesses registered 6 months or less and 48 months of hosting, so it is a creation-stage option only. Both presuppose an entity.
findings.source_quote: La domiciliation de votre entreprise (EI ou micro-entreprise) est obligatoire.

findings.claim: (c) INSEE/INPI rule — whatever address an entrepreneur declares goes into Sirene and the Registre national des entreprises, and is republished on the public Annuaire des entreprises unless he opposes.
findings.detail: INSEE page dated 02/12/2025: the right to object rests on article R123-232-1 of the code de commerce and article 21 GDPR; for a sole proprietorship (catégorie juridique 1000) the withheld fields are name, first names, pseudonym, business name, exact address within the commune and geolocation. Everything else — activity, Siren/Siret, administrative status — keeps being published.
findings.source_quote: Les autres informations concernant l'unité légale restent diffusées

findings.claim: (d) An association loi 1901 does give a publishable address — but the declaration publishes that address in the Journal officiel, so it solves nothing if the siège is his home.
findings.detail: associations.gouv.fr lists the fields of the JOAFE announcement: 'Date de la déclaration en préfecture, Titre de l'association, Objet, Adresse du siège de l'association'. So the association route is only a fix if the siège is somewhere other than his flat — a mairie, a maison des associations, a domiciliation company, or another member's home.
findings.source_quote: Date de la déclaration en préfecture, Titre de l'association, Objet, Adresse du siège de l'association

findings.claim: (d) Cost to create: zero. Declaration and Journal officiel publication have both been free since 2019.
findings.detail: Same page. The receipt arrives within 5 days and publication runs weekly on Tuesdays. The cost that remains is the address itself: free at a member's home or (usually) a mairie, otherwise the ~11–25 €/month domiciliation price above.
findings.source_quote: free since 2019

findings.claim: (d) The declaration also files the administrators' names, professions, addresses and nationality with the préfecture — so his home address reaches the administration even when it is not the siège.
findings.detail: associations.gouv.fr, page dated 16 juin 2025. These fields are declared, not part of the four-field JOAFE announcement, so they are not published in the Journal officiel. Whether they appear in any open-data extract of the RNA I did not verify.
findings.source_quote: Names, professions, addresses, and nationality of administrators

findings.claim: (d) What the association buys him: legal personality — a bank account, contracts, subsidies — i.e. a legal person that can be the newsletter's data controller instead of him personally.
findings.detail: Same page: declaration confers 'la capacité juridique'. Obligations it brings, per the opened pages: written statuts naming title, objet and siège; declaration of the siège and of the administrators; and keeping minutes of deliberations, which the page recommends rather than mandates. The 3-month deadline for declaring changes and the 2-member minimum are widely stated elsewhere but appear on neither page I opened — see unknowns.
findings.source_quote: la capacité juridique

findings.claim: (d) Siège at his own home is lawful — a lease cannot forbid it — but that is exactly the address the Journal officiel would publish.
findings.detail: associations.gouv.fr, 17 juin 2025: for a tenant, 'Un contrat de location ne peut pas interdire à un locataire l'exercice d'une activité associative'; for an owner outside copropriété, 'vous êtes libre de domicilier le siège social de votre association à votre domicile'. Copropriété requires the other owners' agreement when the activity actually happens there.
findings.source_quote: Un contrat de location ne peut pas interdire à un locataire l'exercice d'une activité associative

findings.claim: (e) Yes — a micro-entreprise declared at home publishes that home address by default, and no, it is not unavoidable: an online opposition makes only the commune public.
findings.detail: Service-Public's EI page (verified 2 July 2026) is explicit: 'Seule la commune de résidence sera rendue publique sur le Registre national des entreprises.' The dedicated online service (page dated 25 August 2025) is open to 'toute personne physique inscrite au répertoire Sirene comme entrepreneur individuel', needs FranceConnect and the SIREN, and INSEE processes sole-proprietor requests in 48 hours.
findings.source_quote: Seule la commune de résidence sera rendue publique sur le Registre national des entreprises.

findings.claim: (e) Separate, newer protection: décret n° 2025-840 du 22 août 2025 lets company officers hide their personal address on the RCS, and the INPI states the RNE does not diffuse representatives' personal addresses.
findings.detail: INPI page on anonymisation. This track is aimed at dirigeants de sociétés and at documents filed at the RCS — for a micro-entrepreneur whose établissement is his flat, the Sirene non-diffusion route above is the operative one. The two should not be conflated.
findings.source_quote: Le RNE ne diffuse pas les adresses personnelles des représentants d'entreprises.

findings.claim: (e) TRAP: registering a micro-entreprise puts his address back on the site itself. LCEN mentions légales for an entrepreneur individuel's website require 'votre nom, prénom et adresse'.
findings.detail: Service-Public F31228, 'Vérifié le 31 juillet 2023', with the penalty stated as 1 an d'emprisonnement et 75 000 € d'amende. So INSEE non-diffusion protects the registers, not copius.fr: the day he becomes an EI publishing professionally, he must display an address on the page — which makes a non-home domiciliation a precondition of the micro-entreprise route, not an optional extra.
findings.source_quote: votre nom, prénom et adresse

findings.claim: Today, with no entity, he is not required to publish any address: a non-professional publisher may identify their host instead of themselves.
findings.detail: CNIL, page dated 12 June 2009 — old, but the LCEN regime it describes is unchanged and the CNIL restates the LCEN identification duty on its current pages. The rule as written is an either/or, so his current setup (GitHub Pages named as host, contact@copius.fr, no address) is consistent with it. This is the reason the address problem is a newsletter problem, not a website problem.
findings.source_quote: Le blogueur doit s'identifier ou indiquer le nom de son hébergeur

findings.claim: GDPR-side, the controller's 'coordonnées' in a collection notice need not be postal — the CNIL's own model leaves the channel open.
findings.detail: CNIL example forms, page dated 26 juillet 2019, print the placeholder '[adresse électronique, postale, coordonnées téléphoniques, etc.]' and warn these are illustrations to adapt, not models valid in every case. So the postal address Brevo demanded is an ESP/anti-spam requirement, not something the CNIL's own template forces.
findings.source_quote: [adresse électronique, postale, coordonnées téléphoniques, etc.]

findings.claim: Side finding — copius.fr itself is not leaking his address: AFNIC hides natural-person holders' data from the public Whois by default.
findings.detail: AFNIC expert paper dated 22 April 2021. Worth a 2-minute check that his OVH registration is flagged 'personne physique' rather than published on request, since the default only holds for that flag.
findings.source_quote: the personal data of domain name holders who are natural persons are not published in the directory service available to the general public

research.bottom_line: He can run a newsletter as a private individual — nothing in the address rules requires a company, and as a non-professional publisher he owes no published address for the site itself. The blocker is narrower than it looked: Brevo's onboarding, not the law. The address market, though, is closed to him as he stands. A domiciliation commerciale costs 11–25 € HT/month (SeDomicilier, 8 July 2026; LegalPlace, 18 May 2026) but is sold to a business, existing or in registration — with no entity he can only buy a mail box, which its own vendor says is not a valid address. That leaves three real routes. (1) Do nothing structural: keep the newsletter off, or find an ESP that accepts an email-only footer — the CNIL's own model notice does not force a postal address. (2) Association loi 1901: free to create, free to publish, gives a legal person to own the list — but the Journal officiel publishes the siège address, so it only helps if the siège sits at a mairie, a maison des associations or a paid domiciliation, never at his flat. (3) Micro-entreprise: his home would be published by default, and that is avoidable in the registers (only the commune stays public after the INSEE opposition, verified 2 July 2026) — but it backfires on the site, because an entrepreneur individuel's mentions légales must carry 'votre nom, prénom et adresse'. Since he sells nothing before June 2027, the cheapest correct order is: decide the entity question first, take the address second. Buying an address now is not possible, and creating a micro-entreprise now would publish more than it hides.
unknowns: La Poste boîte postale price for 2026 — the rental page carries no figure and the 2026 tariff documents I searched did not surface a BP line. Needs a bureau de poste or the full catalogue PDF.

Whether Brevo specifically mandates a postal address in the campaign footer, and whether it accepts a domiciliation or mail-box address. I did not open a help.brevo.com page stating the rule; the only Brevo text I saw was a blog post framing it as worldwide anti-spam compliance. Worth one direct check before assuming the blocker is real.
Whether a mail-forwarding box for individuals may lawfully be printed as the contact address of a newsletter — that is the provider's CGV, not a register rule. No provider CGV opened.
Whether a public lycée or a BTS school would host an association siège or a business address, and under what convention. No source found either way.
The loi 1901 minimum of 2 members and the 3-month deadline to declare changes: neither appeared on the government pages I opened, and legifrance refuses WebFetch. Verify before relying on them.

Whether the mairie / maison des associations route is free in his commune — associations.gouv.fr's page on it 404s at both URLs I tried; the surviving search text says the conseil municipal sets any rent. Ask the mairie directly.
Whether RNA open data republishes association administrators' addresses (the JOAFE announcement does not, but the declaration files them).

Article 5 of the e-commerce directive 2000/31 on the 'geographic address at which the service provider is established', and whether a free site with no economic activity falls outside it. EUR-Lex returned empty content on two fetch attempts, so I assert nothing about it.

research.lane: LANE 3 — collecting email addresses from a static GitHub Pages site (mechanisms, RGPD, EU residency, Pages-specific breakage, minimum honest build)

findings.claim: GitHub Pages executes no server-side code, so no form handler, no database and no confirmation-link endpoint can live on copius.fr itself.
findings.detail: This is the root constraint behind every mechanism below: the address must leave the Pages origin at the moment of submission — to a third-party form service, an embedded provider form, a function he owns elsewhere, or the visitor's own mail client.
findings.source_quote: GitHub Pages does not support server-side languages such as PHP, Ruby, or Python.

findings.claim: GitHub Pages cannot set HTTP response headers, so a Content-Security-Policy on copius.fr is only possible through a <meta> tag, and frame-ancestors is ignored that way.
findings.detail: GitHub staff (yoannchaudet) answered the standing request in the community discussion; as of comments dated September 2026 it is still unimplemented. Practical effect: if he embeds a third-party form iframe or script, he can restrict it with a meta CSP, but he cannot set header-level CSP, HSTS or CORS policy on his own site.
findings.source_quote: We don't support this feature today so a `meta` tag unfortunately is the only way.

findings.claim: GitHub's own Pages limits page forbids running an online business or e-commerce site there and warns against sensitive transactions — a free newsletter signup is neither, but the handler must sit off-platform regardless.
findings.detail: Same page: repository recommended limit 1 GB, published site no larger than 1 GB, soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB per month, soft limit of 10 builds per hour. Read 2026-09-15. None of these bite for a signup form; the e-commerce clause becomes relevant only if he starts selling (he has ruled that out before June 2027).
findings.source_quote: GitHub Pages is not intended for or allowed to be used as a free web-hosting service to run your online business, e-commerce site

findings.claim: HTTPS on the custom domain is not a problem: GitHub obtains a Let's Encrypt certificate and 'Enforce HTTPS' redirects all HTTP traffic, so an address typed on copius.fr is encrypted in transit.
findings.detail: Caveat from the same docs set: if he uses CAA records at OVH, at least one must allow letsencrypt.org, and extra or wrong DNS records block certificate issuance. The page also states all Pages sites including correctly configured custom domains support HTTPS and HTTPS enforcement.
findings.source_quote: GitHub queues a job to request a TLS certificate from [Let's Encrypt](https://letsencrypt.org/).

findings.claim: Mechanism 1 — third-party form service (Formspree): technically the simplest, but Formspree's published record puts the data in the US and I could not find a DPA, which leaves RGPD Art. 28 and Chapter V unsatisfied on the public record.
findings.detail: Formspree's privacy policy mentions GDPR exactly once, as a link to gdpr-info.eu, and names no Standard Contractual Clauses. https://formspree.io/legal/dpa/ returns HTTP 404. A search summary (not opened) additionally says hosting is AWS US. For him this is the weakest option: he would be the responsable de traitement with a US sous-traitant and no contract he can show.
findings.source_quote: By using the Services, you acknowledge that Formspree will use your information in the United States and any other country where Formspree operates.

findings.claim: Formspree pricing, read 2026-09-15: Free $0/mo with 50 monthly submissions; Personal $10/mo, 200; Professional $20/mo, 2,000.
findings.detail: The free tier would cover a first year of a small atlas newsletter on volume alone. Volume is not the objection — the missing DPA and US residency are.
findings.source_quote: Free: "$0 /mo" with "50" monthly submissions

findings.claim: Mechanism 2 — embedded/hosted provider form (Tally): stores form data in Europe, free, and its DPA is accepted through the terms rather than signed separately.
findings.detail: Two caveats worth naming to him. First, the DPA wording binds 'professional users ... on behalf of their company' — he has no company, so whether that clause reaches a private individual is genuinely unclear. Second, its sub-processor list includes US parties (SendGrid, Mixpanel, Sentry, Stripe) and Cloudflare EU/US, so 'stored in Europe' is not the whole picture. Pricing read 2026-09-15: "Tally gives you unlimited forms and submissions, completely free, as long as you stay within our fair usage guidelines."
findings.source_quote: All Tally form data is encrypted both in transit and at rest, and stored in Europe.

findings.claim: Netlify Forms is not available to a GitHub Pages site: form detection happens when Netlify builds and parses the site's own HTML.
findings.detail: Netlify's docs describe detection as a deploy-time parse of the site Netlify itself built. A site served from GitHub Pages is never parsed, so the feature has nothing to attach to. If he wanted Netlify Forms he would have to move hosting off GitHub Pages entirely.
findings.source_quote: The Netlify build system finds your forms by parsing the HTML of your site when the build completes.

findings.claim: Mechanism 3 — serverless function (Cloudflare Workers): free tier is ample and the DPA is real with EU SCCs, but EU-only processing is an Enterprise paid add-on, so he cannot promise the data stays in the EU.
findings.detail: Workers free plan: "100,000 per day" requests, 10 ms CPU per invocation; Workers Paid has a minimum charge of $5 USD per month (read 2026-09-15). The Cloudflare customer DPA states the customer is Controller and Cloudflare is Processor, with EU SCCs for restricted transfers. But the Data Localization Suite — the thing that pins processing to a region — is an "Enterprise-only paid add-on".
findings.source_quote: the Customer is the Controller (or a Processor processing Personal Data on behalf of a third-party Controller), and Cloudflare is a Processor (or sub-Processor, as applicable).

findings.claim: Cloudflare D1 (the obvious store behind a Worker) offers a Western Europe location hint but explicitly does not guarantee it.
findings.detail: So a Worker+D1 build cannot honestly carry the sentence 'your address is stored in the EU' on the privacy page. It can carry 'stored by Cloudflare, which we have asked to keep the database in Western Europe'.
findings.source_quote: does not guarantee that D1 runs in your preferred location. Instead, it will run in the nearest possible location (by latency) to your preference.

findings.claim: Vercel's free Hobby plan is restricted to non-commercial personal use — which fits copius.fr exactly today, and stops fitting the day he sells.
findings.detail: Vercel's fair-use page defines commercial usage as any deployment used for the financial gain of anyone involved in producing the project, and explicitly notes "Asking for Donations does not fall under commercial usage." A free atlas with no payments, no ads and no affiliate links is inside Hobby now; a paid learning path in 2027 would require Pro.
findings.source_quote: Hobby teams are restricted to non-commercial personal use only. All commercial usage of the platform requires either a Pro or Enterprise plan.

findings.claim: Scaleway Serverless Functions is the EU-native version of the same mechanism: French provider, Paris region, and a free tier far above anything this site will generate.
findings.detail: Pricing page read 2026-09-15 with Paris selected: "1 000 000 requests Free Tier per account and per month", "400 000 GB-s Free Tier per account and per month", then €0.15 per 1M requests. This is the option that lets him write 'the form is handled by a function running in Paris' and have it be true.
findings.source_quote: 1 000 000 requests Free Tier per account and per month

findings.claim: Mechanism 5 — self-hosting the handler on OVH shared hosting, where his mail already lives, costs a couple of euros a month and gives him PHP plus a database in France.
findings.detail: Prices displayed 2026-09-15 (promotional, struck-through original shown first): Starter "2,59 € 1,59 € HT/mois" with 1 site and "1 base de données 250 Mo"; Perso "5,99 € 2,99 € HT/mois" with 15 sites and 5 databases. The page did not state the PHP version explicitly, and did not state server location on the hosting plans (it says 'hébergé en France' for the email products), so treat both as probable-not-proven.
findings.source_quote: Starter: "2,59 € 1,59 € HT/mois" ... "1 base de données 250 Mo"

findings.claim: Mechanism 4 — a mailto: link is the only option with no sous-traitant to contract with, because nothing is collected by him: the visitor's own mail client sends to contact@copius.fr.
findings.detail: Analysis, not a quoted source. Consequences he should hear: no consent artifact is produced automatically (the email itself is the evidence, which is actually decent proof), the address is exposed to scrapers on a public page, and the list is whatever he curates in his OVH mailbox. It is the honest zero-infrastructure starting point and it breaks nothing on GitHub Pages.

findings.claim: No cookie banner is triggered by a plain HTML form; it is triggered by embedding a third-party provider's script or iframe.
findings.detail: CNIL's rule is that anything not strictly necessary to a service the user expressly requested needs prior consent, and the exemption list covers authentication, shopping cart, load balancing, UI personalisation and consent-choice storage — not provider analytics or marketing cookies. So: a form posting to his own endpoint = no banner; a Tally/Brevo embed = check what it drops, and prefer linking out to a provider-hosted page over embedding it in copius.fr.
findings.source_quote: Tous les cookies n'ayant pas pour finalité exclusive de permettre ou faciliter une communication par voie électronique ou n'étant pas strictement nécessaire à la fourniture d'un service de communication en ligne à la demande expresse de l'utilisateur nécessitent le consentement préalable de l'internaute.

findings.claim: Whichever mechanism he picks, the provider is a sous-traitant and Art. 28 requires a contract — which is why the DPA question, not the price, decides between them.
findings.detail: CNIL defines the sous-traitant as the natural or legal person processing data on behalf of the responsable de traitement, and Art. 28 requires the relationship to be governed by a contract setting out object, duration, nature, purpose, data types, categories of persons and the parties' obligations. Scoreboard from what I could open: Cloudflare — DPA published with EU SCCs; Tally — DPA accepted via terms, wording aimed at professional users; Mailjet — DPA on request only; Formspree — none found (404).
findings.source_quote: Le sous-traitant est la personne physique ou morale (entreprise ou organisme public) qui traite des données pour le compte d'un autre organisme (« le responsable de traitement »)

findings.claim: RGPD applies to him despite having no company: the exemption is for strictly personal or domestic activity, and a mailing list attached to a public website is neither.
findings.detail: Article 2(2)(c) excludes processing by a natural person 'dans le cadre d'une activité strictement personnelle ou domestique'. Publishing a bilingual public atlas and mailing its readers is outside that. The corollary is the useful part: a private individual can perfectly well be a responsable de traitement — nothing in the definition requires a company, a micro-entreprise or an association.
findings.source_quote: par une personne physique dans le cadre d'une activité strictement personnelle ou domestique

findings.claim: His home address is not legally forced onto the site: CNIL states that some non-professional sites and blogs are not required to reveal the identity of the person responsible, while the host must always be identifiable.
findings.detail: This is the direct answer to the Brevo blocker. The postal address demanded at Brevo onboarding was Brevo's own signup requirement, not a French legal condition on running a non-commercial newsletter. He would still name the host — GitHub (for the site) and OVHcloud (for the mailbox) — and give contact@copius.fr as his own contact point.
findings.source_quote: Certains sites et blogs non-professionnels ne sont pas tenus par l'obligation de révéler l'identité du responsable du site. Toutefois, l'identification de l'hébergeur est toujours requise

findings.claim: CNIL's mandatory information list asks for the 'identité et coordonnées' of the controller — contact details, with no postal address specified.
findings.detail: The full list he must show at the point of collection: identity and contact details, purposes, legal basis, whether providing the address is optional and the consequences, recipients or categories of recipients, retention period or its criteria, the rights (access, rectification, erasure, limitation), DPO contact if any, and the right to complain to the CNIL — in 'termes clairs et simples'. Note this is an absence of a postal-address requirement rather than an explicit permission to omit one.
findings.source_quote: Identité et coordonnées de l'organisme (responsable du traitement de données)

findings.claim: Prior consent is the rule for electronic prospection, with an exception for non-commercial solicitation — and every message must let the person refuse further contact.
findings.detail: CNIL lists two exceptions to prior consent: an existing customer contacted about similar products, and prospection that is not commercial in nature (their example is charitable). A free atlas selling nothing arguably lands in the second, but the exception still requires informing the person at collection, so the practical design is identical: ask, inform, record. Every message must carry a simple means of refusing further solicitation.
findings.source_quote: La publicité par voie électronique (courrier électronique, SMS-MMS, automate d'appel, etc.) est possible à condition que les personnes aient donné leur consentement avant d'être démarchées.

findings.claim: Consent must be provable, and CNIL itself describes the two-stage collection — a confirmation email the person must act on — which is exactly the double opt-in the minimum build should use.
findings.detail: The page describes consent collected in multiple steps, including an email the person must confirm, and places the burden of proof on the controller to demonstrate at any time that consent was validly given. The fetched page returned this in translation, so treat the two-stage wording as paraphrase; the requirement to document the conditions of collection is stated plainly.
findings.source_quote: be able to demonstrate at any time that the person has indeed consented, under valid conditions

findings.claim: On EU residency: Brevo (OVH France/Germany plus Google Cloud Belgium), Tally (stored in Europe), Scaleway (Paris) and OVH (France) keep data in the EU; Cloudflare only with an Enterprise add-on; Formspree does not.
findings.detail: The Brevo statement comes from a staff reply on Brevo's community forum, not from a legal document — treat it as good but not contractual evidence. Mailjet's free plan (read 2026-09-15) is 6,000 emails/month, 200/day, 1,000 contacts, and its DPA is request-only ('You can contact us on privacy@mailjet.com should you wish to obtain this DPA'); I could not open its help-centre page on storage location, so its EU hosting is unverified here.
findings.source_quote: the servers of our hosting providers (GCP and OVH) are all located in the European Union (Belgium and France)

findings.claim: Minimum honest implementation: a static form on copius.fr posting to a function he owns in France, which records a pending address, emails a confirmation link, and only then writes the address to a list he holds.
findings.detail: Concretely: (1) plain HTML form, one email field plus an unticked checkbox whose label is the consent wording, no third-party script, no cookie, so no banner; (2) POST to a Scaleway function in Paris (free tier) or a PHP script on OVH shared hosting (~€1.59–2.99 HT/mo, read 2026-09-15) — either is an endpoint he controls in the EU; (3) the endpoint stores address, timestamp, and the exact consent wording shown, in a pending state, and mails a confirmation link; (4) only a clicked link promotes the row to confirmed — that click is his proof of consent; (5) every newsletter carries an unsubscribe link and contact@copius.fr; (6) the privacy page gets rewritten in both languages the same day the form ships, naming himself as responsable de traitement with contact@copius.fr, the hosts (GitHub for the site, OVHcloud for mail, Scaleway or OVH for the endpoint), the purpose, the legal basis, the retention rule and the rights. Zero-infrastructure fallback if he wants to start this week: a mailto: link and a text file — no processor, no contract, no banner. Note that a cross-origin POST by fetch() needs the endpoint to return Access-Control-Allow-Origin for https://copius.fr, while a classic form submit does not; I did not verify that against a spec page in this pass.

unknowns: Brevo's postal-address demand at onboarding: help.brevo.com returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch, so I could not read the account-verification or anti-spam policy page. Gabriel's first-hand account of hitting it in September 2026 stands as the record.
Whether Tally's DPA binds a non-professional account holder — its GDPR page says 'professional users also agree, on behalf of their company', and he has no company.
Whether Tally's embedded form drops cookies on the embedding page — their GDPR page says nothing about cookies. Linking out to a Tally-hosted page instead of embedding sidesteps this.
Mailjet's data storage location: documentation.mailjet.com returns HTTP 403; only a search summary (GCP Frankfurt and Saint-Ghislain) supports EU hosting, and a search summary is not a source.
Whether Formspree has any DPA at all: https://formspree.io/legal/dpa/ is a 404 and the privacy policy names no SCCs. Absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

The CNIL three-year retention rule for prospection data (three years from last contact from the prospect): the référentiel PDF downloaded but its text could not be extracted, so I did not read the sentence. It is widely cited but unquoted here.
Whether Vercel Hobby lets a function be pinned to the fra1 (Paris) region — not checked.
Netlify's explicit statement that Forms requires Netlify hosting: inferred from the deploy-time-parse sentence in their docs, not read as a standalone sentence.
OVH shared hosting: the pricing page did not state the PHP version or the server location for the Eco plans; 'hébergé en France' appeared only against the email products.
research.bottom_line: Yes, he can run a newsletter right now, as a private individual with no company. Nothing in RGPD requires a legal entity to be a responsable de traitement, and CNIL states that some non-professional sites and blogs need not reveal the identity of the person responsible while the host must always be identifiable — so his home address was Brevo's signup requirement, not French law. What the static site actually forces is only this: GitHub Pages runs no server-side language and cannot set HTTP headers, so the address must leave copius.fr on submission. Of the five mechanisms, a third-party form service is the fastest and worst (Formspree processes in the US with no DPA I could find), Netlify Forms is simply unavailable to a Pages site, Cloudflare Workers has a real DPA but EU residency only on an Enterprise add-on, and the two that let him say something true about where the data lives are a Scaleway function in Paris (1M free requests/month) or PHP on OVH shared hosting alongside the mailbox he already has (~€1.59–2.99 HT/mo, read 2026-09-15). The minimum honest build is a plain HTML form with an unticked consent box, posting to that EU endpoint, which stores the address as pending and mails a confirmation link — the click is the proof of consent CNIL requires him to be able to produce — with an unsubscribe link in every send. No third-party script means no cookie banner. The one thing that must ship the same day as the form is the rewritten privacy page in both languages; leaving 'there is no form, no mailing list' up while a form is live is the only part of this that would be dishonest.

findings.claim: Brevo's Terms of Service forbid non-professional use outright — this is the one provider whose terms require a business, and it is why his September 2026 signup stalled.
findings.source_quote: You also agree to use our Services for the sole purpose of your professional activity, excluding any use as a non-professional or consumer.
findings.detail: Clause 1.3 'User agreement', in the version the page labels 'Version : October 1st, 2025'. Clause 1.4 adds that you declare you are 'authorized to act on behalf of the legal entity that You represent'. Gabriel has no legal entity and is publishing a free site as a private individual, so he cannot truthfully accept these terms. Note the contradiction with Brevo's own pricing page, which markets the free plan as 'Free forever, no credit card needed Best for individuals and solopreneurs building an online presence' (https://www.brevo.com/pricing/) — the marketing copy invites exactly the user the contract excludes. FLAGGED: Brevo is the only provider of the eight whose terms require a registered business/professional activity.

findings.claim: EmailOctopus explicitly admits consumers — individuals buying for personal, non-business use — as a contracting party.
findings.source_quote: be a business or a consumer able to enter into valid contracts;
findings.detail: Terms of Use and Anti-Spam Policy, 'Eligibility' section, page states 'Last updated: 31 March 2022'. The terms go further and define the category: 'You are a consumer if: 1. You are an individual. 2. You are buying a service from us wholly or mainly for your personal use (not for use in connection with your trade, business, craft or profession).' No SIRET, company number, or VAT number is required. EmailOctopus is Three Hearts Digital Ltd, 86-90 Paul Street, London EC2A 4NE, UK.

findings.claim: EmailOctopus is the only provider found that will substitute its own address for his in the sent email, so he gives them his home address privately but subscribers never see it.
findings.source_quote: If you work from home or simply don't want your subscribers to know your address then with EmailOctopus you can opt to keep the address private in your emails.
findings.detail: Page states 'Last updated on April 5, 2026'. The same article sets the condition: 'Make sure you provide your real address in the form, though, we'll need to be able to forward on any correspondence sent to us.' So the real address is disclosed to EmailOctopus only, not published. The setting is called Private Address and lives in the sender info screen. Caveat stated on the page: 'You can only use our Private Address functionality for emails sent through the EmailOctopus platform.' This directly answers the objection that killed the Brevo signup.

findings.claim: EmailOctopus stores subscriber lists in Ireland, inside the EEA.
findings.source_quote: Your contact lists are stored in Ireland, within the European Economic Area ("EEA"), on the secure servers of Amazon Web Services ("AWS").
findings.detail: The privacy policy separately confirms account data: 'The account details and IP address that we collect from you are stored on our AWS servers in Ireland, inside the UK and European Economic Area ("EEA").' It also discloses that staff and sub-processors may operate outside the UK/EEA. This is the best data-residency answer of any hosted provider here bar Brevo (France) and Ghost (Amsterdam).

findings.claim: EmailOctopus's Data Processing Terms are conditioned on the customer being a business — which leaves a genuine gap for a private individual who is still a GDPR data controller.
findings.source_quote: Data processing terms To the extent that you are a business and we process personal data on your behalf in providing the Services, the Data Processing Terms shall apply and are incorporated into these Terms.
findings.detail: Clause 23. Running a public newsletter is not covered by GDPR's purely-personal-activity exemption, so Gabriel would be a controller and Article 28 would normally require a processor contract. EmailOctopus's own DPA hook only fires 'to the extent that you are a business'. In practice this is a paperwork gap, not a blocker to signing up, and he can ask them to execute the Data Processing Terms anyway. I did not find a separate standalone DPA URL that resolves (emailoctopus.com/legal/data-processing returns 404); there is a 'GDPR' link in their footer I did not open.

findings.claim: Buttondown publishes its own corporate address for customers to use in their newsletter footer, and its signup asks only for username, email and password — no postal address at onboarding.
findings.source_quote: Use our official newsletter address. Like our friends at ConvertKit, Buttondown offers a physical address:
findings.detail: The address given on that page is '304 S. Jones Blvd #3567, Las Vegas NV 89107'. The same page is blunt about the home-address problem: 'Don't use your actual home's address. Rent a P.O. box, an office, or something along those lines.' and notes 'Buttondown doesn't do any enforcement or analysis of your address.' Separately, Buttondown's own getting-started docs (https://docs.buttondown.com/) list the signup inputs as username, email address and password only — no postal address is requested to create the account. Caveat: the blog post is dated 2020-03-01, so the specific Las Vegas address should be re-checked in-app before use.

findings.claim: Mailchimp requires a real mail-receiving postal address in every marketing email and offers no address-substitution feature — the burden is pushed entirely onto the sender.
findings.source_quote: Votre adresse postale — Adresse où recevoir des plis postaux ; il ne peut s'agir d'une adresse électronique ou d'un site Web. Si vous travaillez à domicile et ne souhaitez pas partager votre adresse personnelle, nous vous suggérons d'utiliser une boîte postale.
findings.detail: Mailchimp geo-redirects to French for a French IP; this is the 'Contenu obligatoire du bas de page' section, which opens 'Conformément aux lois anti-spam et à nos Conditions d'utilisation, vous devez inclure certaines informations dans chaque e-mail que vous envoyez.' Mailchimp's separate article 'Idées d'adresse physique alternative' (https://mailchimp.com/help/alternative-physical-address-ideas/) lists workarounds — a manager's PO box, a studio, a gallery affiliation — and concludes 'Parfois, la seule réponse est d'acheter une boîte postale.' Mailchimp's answer to a home-address objection is therefore 'go rent a PO box', not 'use ours'.

findings.claim: Mailchimp's free tier in 2026 is 250 contacts and 500 sends per month, with a 250/day cap — far tighter than EmailOctopus's free tier.
findings.source_quote: The Free plan includes up to 250 contacts and 500 sends per month, with a daily send limit of 250.
findings.detail: The free plan also gives 1 audience and 1 seat. Overage behaviour is stated on the same page: 'If you exceed the 250 contact limit in your Free plan, a hold is placed on sending live emails or test emails until you upgrade to a paid plan or reduce your contact total.' The first paid step is Essentials, where 'The starting price includes up to 500 contacts, and the price increases with your contact total.' I could not extract a reliable Essentials euro price — the pricing page renders its numbers via JavaScript and the static HTML contains only an unattached '17'/'38' pair, so I am not asserting a figure.

findings.claim: EmailOctopus's free tier is the most generous of the hosted options — 2,500 subscribers and 10,000 emails/month — but it forces a referral link into every email on top of the address.
findings.source_quote: STARTER Free 2,500 subscribers 10,000 emails per month EmailOctopus branding on emails Reports available for 30 days Create 1 landing page and 1 form Access for 1 user
findings.detail: The first paid step is 'PRO $9 PER MONTH, BILLED YEARLY' which removes branding and gives unlimited landing pages and forms. The free-tier footer obligation is spelled out separately at https://help.emailoctopus.com/article/222-whats-required-in-a-footer (page dated 'Last updated on June 25, 2026'): 'Do you use our free Starter plan? If so, we require all free accounts to add a Rewards link to your campaigns.' The same page confirms the free plan still includes '1 landing page and 1 form' — which is exactly the mechanism a static site needs.

findings.claim: Ghost has no free tier at all; the cheapest hosted plan is $18 USD/month billed yearly, which is the wrong shape for a project with no revenue until June 2027.
findings.source_quote: Starter For solo blogs & newsletters $18 USD / mo Billed yearly
findings.detail: The Starter plan is capped at 1,000 members; the next step is 'Publisher For custom publications $29 USD / mo Billed yearly'. The 'Try for free' buttons are a trial, not a free tier. Ghost's source code is open and self-hostable at no licence cost, but self-hosting needs a server and a separate bulk-mail relay, which Gabriel does not have. Over 21 months to June 2027, Starter alone is roughly $378.

findings.claim: Ghost hosts its customer data in the EU — Amsterdam — which is the strongest residency answer of the hosted options after Brevo.
findings.source_quote: Ghost Foundation's servers are located in Amsterdam, The Netherlands.
findings.detail: The same policy notes 'These third party vendors and hosting partners may be located in a country other than The Netherlands or your country of residence.' Ghost's footer links a dedicated 'Data Processing' policy page; the URLs I tried for it (ghost.org/help/data-processing/ and /help/data-processing-addendum/) both 404, so I did not read the DPA itself.

findings.claim: Substack is a US company under California law and takes the reader relationship — the subscriber list is not really his, which is a strategic cost separate from any address question.
findings.source_quote: These Terms are governed by and will be construed under applicable federal law and the laws of the State of California, without regard to the conflicts of laws provisions thereof.
findings.detail: Terms of Use show 'Effective date: April 21, 2025'. Disputes go to 'arbitration in San Francisco County, California'. The privacy policy (https://substack.com/privacy) shows Substack relies on the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework for EU personal data and appoints Bird & Bird as its EU representative at 'Zuid-Hollandplein 22, 2596 AW The Hague, The Netherlands'. Publishing is free and Substack only takes a cut on paid subscriptions, which is moot since he sells nothing. But Substack is a controller in its own right, not a processor working for him, and the newsletter lives on substack.com rather than copius.fr.

findings.claim: I could NOT verify Substack's postal-address behaviour from a primary source — its support site blocks automated fetches.
findings.detail: support.substack.com returns HTTP 403 to every fetch I attempted. Search summaries claim Substack shows a mailing address at the bottom of all emails and that it may be a PO Box editable in publication settings, but a search summary is not a source and I am not asserting it. He should check this himself in Substack's settings before relying on it. Treat Substack's answers to (a) and (b) as unverified.

findings.claim: I could NOT verify Brevo's onboarding address screen from a primary source — Brevo's help centre returns 403 to every fetch.
findings.detail: help.brevo.com returned HTTP 403 across en-us, en-gb and fr locales and with browser headers and a referer. Gabriel's own first-hand account — that onboarding demanded a postal address and he abandoned there — stands as the record here, and it is consistent with what I could verify: Brevo's anti-spam policy (https://www.brevo.com/legal/antispampolicy/) makes the customer 'solely responsible for ... complying with all applicable sender-identification, disclosure, and content requirements (including under CAN-SPAM and the TSR)'. But the specific question of whether Brevo prints that address in every message is unverified from source. It is also moot: the professional-use clause rules Brevo out before the address question is reached.

findings.claim: Brevo's free tier is 300 emails/day and its data controller for a French user is a French company, with a DPA built into the terms as Appendix 3.
findings.source_quote: When you create an account, you will automatically have a Free plan to upload your contacts. Once we approve your account for sending, you can start sending up to 300 emails per day.
findings.detail: Brevo's privacy policy (https://www.brevo.com/legal/privacypolicy/) names the parent as 'Sendinblue, a French société par actions simplifiée, whose registered office is located at 17 rue Salneuve, 75017 Paris, France' and says 'Depending on your location, the data controller may be Sendinblue France (SAS), Sendinblue North-America (Inc.) or Sendinblue Germany (GmbH).' The DPA is Appendix 3 of the Terms of Service, so no separate signature is needed. The first paid step is the Starter plan, 'From 5,000 emails per month' — the price renders via JavaScript and the static HTML says only 'Loading content...', so I am not quoting a figure. All academic given the eligibility bar.

findings.claim: Listmonk is genuinely free and imposes no terms on him at all, but it is the wrong tool for his situation — it needs a server he does not have.
findings.source_quote: listmonk is free and open source software licensed under AGPLv3.
findings.detail: Self-hosted, 'Performance and features packed into a single binary', installed with './listmonk --install to setup the Postgres DB'. There is no vendor, so questions (a), (b) and (e) do not arise: no onboarding address, no forced footer, no eligibility clause. Question (c) becomes wherever he rents the box. The real cost is not the licence: he would need a VPS, a Postgres database, a separate SMTP relay (which will have its own terms and its own address demands), plus SPF/DKIM alignment and bounce handling, and he would personally become the sender of record. For a student with zero subscribers today, the machinery is larger than the thing it serves.

findings.claim: OVHcloud does offer its own customers a mailing-list feature, but it is a Sympa-style discussion/announce list, not a newsletter platform — and OVH itself warns against using it for mass marketing.
findings.source_quote: A mailing list is not a solution designed for sending spam (advertising emails) en masse. This type of usage is tolerated to a certain degree, provided that it is not used in an abusive manner.
findings.detail: Guide 'Managing and using mailing lists', front-matter shows 'lastUpdated: 2025-04-28'. Requirements: 'an MX Plan 100 minimum or web hosting plan eligible for mailing lists'. Gabriel has a mailbox at OVH but the site is on GitHub Pages, so whether his current plan qualifies is unknown. Functionally it manages subscribers and moderation ('A moderated mailing list is useful for sending newsletters, for example') but gives him no signup form, no double opt-in flow, no unsubscribe-link management and no templates — he would still have to build subscription capture himself, which is the exact thing a static site cannot do. No business status is required; it is a hosting feature. OVH email starts at '0,30 € HT/mois/compte' (https://www.ovhcloud.com/fr/emails/).

findings.claim: French law does not require him to publish a postal address on copius.fr itself — the CNIL states non-professional site publishers are exempt from revealing their identity.
findings.source_quote: Certains sites et blogs non-professionnels ne sont pas tenus par l'obligation de révéler l'identité du responsable du site. Toutefois, l'identification de l'hébergeur est toujours requise, mais celui-ci - astreint au secret professionnel - ne peut a priori pas vous communiquer d'informations sur le responsable du site.
findings.detail: This matters because it separates two things he may be conflating. The address that appears in a newsletter footer is a PROVIDER policy, driven by the US CAN-SPAM Act and written into every ESP's terms — not a French requirement on his website. The site itself, as a free non-professional publication, can name its host (GitHub) without naming him. Note the hedge in the CNIL's own wording: 'Certains sites et blogs non-professionnels' — some, not all. I marked this medium because legifrance is unfetchable and I could not read LCEN article 6 III directly to confirm the exact boundary of the exemption.

findings.claim: Collecting addresses from a static site needs no backend — the provider hosts the form, and EmailOctopus's free tier already includes one.
findings.source_quote: Due to anti-spam laws and our Terms of Use, there are a few things that you must include in there.
findings.detail: The mechanism: the ESP gives him either an embeddable HTML form that posts directly to the ESP's own endpoint, or a fully provider-hosted landing page he links to from copius.fr. Neither needs a server, a database, or anything GitHub Pages cannot serve — the subscriber's browser talks to EmailOctopus, not to him. EmailOctopus's free Starter tier includes exactly 'Create 1 landing page and 1 form' (https://emailoctopus.com/pricing), and Pro lifts that to unlimited. Consequence he must not miss: the privacy page on copius.fr currently states in both languages that there is no form, no mailing list and no analytics. The moment a form goes live that statement is false and must be rewritten — new purpose, new legal basis (consent), new processor, new retention period, new withdrawal route.

unknowns: Brevo's onboarding flow itself — help.brevo.com returns 403 to all automated fetches, so his first-hand account of the address demand is the only record. Moot anyway: the professional-use clause excludes him before that screen.
Substack's postal-address behaviour — support.substack.com returns 403. Whether Substack prints an address in every email, and whether a PO box is accepted, is unverified from source.

Exact euro prices for Brevo Starter, Mailchimp Essentials, and Buttondown above 100 subscribers. All three render prices via JavaScript; the static HTML carries only placeholder text or unattached numbers. Verified prices: EmailOctopus Pro $9/mo billed yearly, Ghost Starter $18 USD/mo billed yearly, OVH email €0.30 HT/mo per account.

Whether Gabriel's current OVH plan qualifies for mailing lists. The guide requires 'an MX Plan 100 minimum or web hosting plan eligible for mailing lists'; he has a mailbox but the site is on GitHub Pages. He must check his OVH control panel.

Mailchimp's and Buttondown's data-residency detail and DPA terms. Both are US-domiciled (Intuit; Buttondown LLC, Richmond VA) and Buttondown's privacy policy references a DPA, but I did not open either DPA document.

Whether EmailOctopus will execute its Data Processing Terms with a customer who is a consumer rather than a business — clause 23 is conditioned on business status. Worth one support email before he commits.

The exact boundary of the LCEN non-professional publisher exemption. legifrance.gouv.fr refuses automated fetches and the EUR-Lex HTML endpoint returned an empty 202, so I could not read LCEN art. 6 III or e-Commerce Directive 2000/31 art. 5-6 in primary text.
Whether the Las Vegas address Buttondown published in 2020 is still the address it offers in 2026 — the blog post is six years old and should be confirmed in-app.
research.bottom_line:
Yes, he can run a newsletter right now, as a private individual with no SIRET — and the specific thing that stopped him at Brevo is solvable at two providers.

The Brevo abandonment was correct, and for a better reason than he knew. Brevo's terms bar him outright: "You also agree to use our Services for the sole purpose of your professional activity, excluding any use as a non-professional or consumer" (ToS 1.3, version dated 1 October 2025). That is the only provider of the eight whose terms require a business. He should not go back to it, address problem or not.

RECOMMENDATION: EmailOctopus. It is the only provider that answers all five questions the way he needs. Its terms admit "a business or a consumer", defining a consumer as an individual buying "wholly or mainly for your personal use" — no SIRET, no company. A postal address is still required in the footer, as it is everywhere, but EmailOctopus is the one provider that will hide it: "If you work from home or simply don't want your subscribers to know your address then with EmailOctopus you can opt to keep the address private in your emails" (help article, updated 5 April 2026). He gives them his home address privately; subscribers never see it. Subscriber lists sit in Ireland, inside the EEA. The free tier carries 2,500 subscribers and 10,000 emails/month — more than he will need before June 2027 — and includes one hosted landing page and one form. First paid step $9/month billed yearly.

FALLBACK: Buttondown, which publishes its own address for customers to use in their footer and asks for no postal address at signup. US-hosted, so weaker on data residency, and the published address dates from a 2020 post that needs confirming in-app.

RULED OUT: Brevo (business-only). Mailchimp (250 contacts free, and its answer to the home-address problem is "go rent a PO box"). Ghost ($18/month minimum, no free tier — wrong shape with no revenue). Substack (US-controlled, takes the reader relationship, moves his brand off copius.fr). Listmonk (free software, but needs a VPS, Postgres and an SMTP relay he does not have — the machinery outweighs the list). OVHcloud (real feature, but an announce-list, not a newsletter tool: no signup form, no double opt-in, and OVH itself says mass marketing is only "tolerated to a certain degree").

ON COLLECTION FROM A STATIC SITE: this is a non-problem. The ESP hosts the form; the subscriber's browser posts to the ESP, not to him. GitHub Pages serves an embedded form or a link to a provider-hosted landing page, and no backend is ever involved.

TWO THINGS TO SEPARATE. The footer address is a provider policy driven by the US CAN-SPAM Act, not a French obligation on his website — the CNIL states non-professional sites and blogs "ne sont pas tenus par l'obligation de révéler l'identité du responsable du site", though the host must be identifiable. So copius.fr can stay address-free while the newsletter still needs a footer address, and EmailOctopus supplies one.

ONE THING HE MUST NOT SKIP: his privacy page says, in both languages, that there is no form, no mailing list and no analytics. The day a signup form goes live that becomes false. It has to be rewritten first — new purpose, consent as legal basis, a named processor, a retention period, and how to withdraw — not after the first subscriber arrives.

verdicts.claim: The LCEN site-identification duty is no longer "article 6-III" — since 23 May 2024 it sits in article 1-1 of loi n° 2004-575, and article 6 now covers intermediaries only.
verdicts.why: Légifrance prints Article 1-1 of loi n° 2004-575 with heading "Version en vigueur depuis le 23/05/2024", and its section I opens with the éditeur identification duty. The consolidated law confirms article 6 now runs on intermediaries (providers, hosts, platforms, data retention) with no éditeur-identification III. Nothing here is specific to professionals, so it binds him the same way. Stale citation, unchanged substance — exactly as stated.

verdicts.claim: (a) The non-professional publisher's anonymity regime survived the renumbering intact: Gabriel may publish only GitHub's name and address, not his own, provided he has given GitHub his identity.
verdicts.why: The quoted sentence is verbatim and sits in section II of article 1-1, with the secret professionnel clause and the "non opposable à l'autorité judiciaire" carve-out both present. But the condition is not 'GitHub holds his account identity' — the text requires him to have communicated "les éléments d'identification personnelle mentionnés au I", and section I for a personne physique is literally "leurs nom, prénoms, domicile et numéro de téléphone". A default GitHub account holds a username and an email address. Username plus email is not nom, prénoms, domicile and téléphone, so on the face of the text the anonymity option is not yet available to him. Second untested point: article 1-1 imposes French professional secrecy on the hébergeur, and GitHub is a US company that has made him no such undertaking — if GitHub declines to hold or to protect those details, the paragraph has nothing to stand on.
