verdicts.correction: Before relying on section II, he must actually give the host nom, prénoms, domicile and numéro de téléphone and keep proof he did. Until then, publish the full mentions légales or move the site to a host that accepts and acknowledges those four items.

verdicts.claim: (a) The CPCE prospection régime does not bite today: "prospection directe" is defined as promoting goods, services, or the image of a person who SELLS goods or provides services. Gabriel sells nothing, so article L34-5's opt-in rule is not triggered by a free editorial letter.
verdicts.why: The definition sentence is verbatim in L34-5 (third paragraph; version en vigueur depuis le 26 juillet 2020), and the first paragraph does prohibit prospection directe toward "une personne physique qui n'a pas exprimé préalablement son consentement". So the régime is commercial by construction — that much is right, and it is the load-bearing claim of the whole memo. What does not follow is 'not triggered'. The definition catches promotion "directement ou indirectement" of "des biens, des services ou l'image d'une personne vendant des biens" — it does not say the seller has to be the sender. A culinary letter that names producers, wines, books, shops or restaurants, or links to them, promotes indirectly the goods of persons who sell goods, and that reading is available to a regulator on the text alone. I found no CNIL or DGCCRF decision holding a free third-party-free editorial letter outside L34-5; the conclusion rests on reading, not on authority. Two further points the claim does not carry: enforcement of L34-5 runs through the consumer code agents (L. 511-3, L. 511-21) and the DGCCRF, not only the CNIL, so CNIL's non-commercial doctrine is not a defence before that authority; and his own freemium plan (free atlas, paid learning path) means the premise 'nothing for sale' has a shelf-life measured in months.
verdicts.correction: State it as: L34-5 is commercial by construction and probably does not reach a letter that promotes nobody's goods — and keep the letter genuinely free of third-party sellers, links and product placement, or the 'indirectement' limb reaches it.

verdicts.claim: (a,b) Even where L34-5 DOES apply, it requires "coordonnées valables" for opting out and a non-concealed sender identity — it never says "adresse postale".
verdicts.why: The quoted paragraph is verbatim on the Légifrance page, both prohibitions intact, plus the ban on a subject line unrelated to the service offered. The word adresse does not appear in it. This paragraph opens "Dans tous les cas", so it is the one limb of L34-5 that does not depend on consent — worth knowing, because it is the part that would bind him first if the definition question in the previous claim ever went against him. A working unsubscribe link plus a monitored reply-to satisfies it.

verdicts.claim: (a,b) CNIL's own rule for NON-commercial prospection is opt-out, not opt-in: inform the person and let them object simply and free of charge.
verdicts.why: The CNIL prospection page carries the carve-out with both conditions: the person must "être informée" that the address will be used for prospection "non commerciale", and "être en mesure de s'opposer à cette utilisation de manière simple et gratuite lorsque les données sont collectées, et à tout moment notamment lors de chaque envoi". Two points the claim's rendering flattens: CNIL's own example is caritative, and it attaches the objection right both at collection and at every send, not just at collection. The advice to take a real opt-in anyway is the right call — it is strictly stronger than what CNIL asks, and it is what he has to prove under article 7(1) regardless.

verdicts.claim: (b) What CNIL actually requires INSIDE the message is two things: the sender's identity, and a simple way to refuse. Nothing else.
verdicts.why: Verbatim on the cited page, which resolves and is dated 10 juin 2026: each solicitation must let the person know "l'identité de l'organisation qui l'émet" and express "par un moyen simple, son refus de recevoir de nouvelles sollicitations". Note this URL and the one cited two claims earlier are the same CNIL page, so the memo's 'two prospection pages' is one page counted twice — relevant to the independence of the negative claim below. 'Nothing else' is true of the message body only: the RGPD information duty still bites at the point of collection, which is the subscribe box, not the letter.

verdicts.claim: (b) No French text I opened requires a postal address inside a newsletter message. I checked all four candidate homes and none contains one.
verdicts.why: Each source checks out: L34-5 says coordonnées valables and never adresse; the CNIL prospection page has no occurrence of adresse postale and treats postal prospection as a separate topic; the règles d'or page requires only "le nom et les coordonnées du responsable du traitement" on the désinscription page; article 1-1 LCEN governs the site. Two weaknesses in the evidence, neither fatal. The règles d'or page is dated 16 juin 2009 — it predates the RGPD entirely, so it is a weak authority to rest a negative on. And the four homes are really three, because two of the URLs are the same CNIL page. The conclusion still holds for everything I opened.

verdicts.claim: The postal-address demand he hit is a US CAN-SPAM rule, not a French one: the FTC requires a valid physical postal address in every commercial email.
verdicts.why: The FTC quote is verbatim, and the diagnosis of why a US-facing platform demands it is sound. Two corrections. First, the FTC guide gives no support for the aside that a free editorial letter is not a commercial message — the guide's test is the message's primary purpose, it says the Act "covers all commercial messages" and carves out no exception for newsletters or for informational content. Since the rule reaches any US-resident subscriber on his list, 'CAN-SPAM does not apply to me' is an assertion he would be making, not one the source makes. Second, and this is the practical half: Brevo's demand binds him as a contract term whether or not a law stands behind it. Concluding 'no French law requires this' does not get him past the wall — it only tells him which argument will not work with support.
verdicts.correction: Frame it as: no French text requires it, and the platform requires it under its own terms. If he wants to avoid publishing an address in the footer, the fix is a domiciliation or BP address, or an ESP whose terms do not demand one — not an appeal to French law.

verdicts.claim: (c) Selling flips three separate switches at once, and the first is the one he will not see coming: his home address becomes publishable.
verdicts.why: The direction is right and the first switch is the important one. But the third leg is built on a citation with problems. Article 19 LCEN at the cited LEGIARTI is marked in force from 01/07/2016 only until 01/01/2027 — so it expires before he plausibly starts selling, and a memo that just flagged stale citations should not rest on one with a known end date. The quoted sentence also starts mid-sentence: the article opens "Sans préjudice des autres obligations d'information prévues par les textes législatifs et réglementaires en vigueur", which the quote silently drops. The enumerated items (email, telephone, registry number) I did not verify item by item. On the first leg: article 1-1 I 1° says literally "domicile" for a personne physique, so a domiciliation address is the practical answer rather than a textually airtight one. And the memo misses the cheap half of the privacy fix — service-public states an entrepreneur individuel "peut demander la non-diffusion publique de son adresse personnelle" in the registre, which is free and independent of any domiciliation contract.
verdicts.correction: Re-cite article 19 to its current version and check its end date before relying on it; add the free RNE non-diffusion request alongside the domiciliation, since the two solve different exposures (registre vs. mentions légales).

verdicts.claim: (d) The right RGPD basis is consent, article 6(1)(a) — and he must be able to demonstrate it, with withdrawal as easy as giving it.
verdicts.why: Both articles are on the CNIL page as quoted. Article 7(3) ends literally "Il est aussi simple de retirer que de donner son consentement." Article 7(1) reads "le responsable du traitement est en mesure de démontrer" — indicative, not the "doit pouvoir" of the paraphrase; same effect, but quote it as it reads. Two softer points: 'the right basis' is a recommendation rather than a legal finding, and CNIL's own non-commercial carve-out implies opt-out on legitimate interest would also be lawful for him — consent is the better choice, not the only lawful one. The parenthetical that CNIL's own newsletter runs on 6(1)(e) I could not verify; the page that would carry it 404s. The advice not to copy CNIL's wording is sound regardless.

verdicts.claim: (d) The privacy notice must carry nine items, and his current page — "no form, no mailing list, no analytics" — becomes false the day a subscribe box ships.
verdicts.why: The nine items are on the CNIL page as listed, and the delivery standard is verbatim: "concise, transparente, compréhensible et aisément accessible, en des termes clairs et simples". The list is incomplete for his case. CNIL carries a second block of mentions required "selon les cas", and one of them is the droit de retrait du consentement — which applies precisely because the previous claim puts him on consent. His notice needs that tenth line, not nine. On the DPO item: CNIL marks it conditional, "s'il a été désigné". He has none, so the item does not apply; writing a line to say so is a style preference, not a requirement, and the memo states it as though it were one.
verdicts.correction: Ten items for a consent-based list: the nine, plus the right to withdraw consent at any time. Drop the instruction to write a 'no DPO' line, or mark it as optional.

verdicts.claim: (d) Yes, he needs a registre des traitements — the small-entity exemption does not cover a standing mailing list, because that processing is not occasional.
verdicts.why: The CNIL quotes are verbatim: the obligation "concerne tous les organismes, publics comme privés et quelle que soit leur taille", and sub-250 entities must still record "les traitements non occasionnels", risky processing, and sensitive data. The conclusion holds, but the route is the wrong one and should be fixed before he relies on it. The CNIL page addresses organismes and says nothing about a private individual, so applying it to him is an extrapolation. The cleaner route reaches the same place more firmly: article 30(1) RGPD binds every responsable du traitement, and the 30(5) exemption is drafted for "une entreprise ou une organisation comptant moins de 250 employés" — a natural person is arguably neither, so the exemption never opens for him at all. Either way: one page, and it is not optional.
verdicts.correction: Ground it on article 30(1) and 30(5) directly rather than on a CNIL page written for organismes.

verdicts.claim: (e) Double opt-in is not legally required in France. No text imposes it, and none of the CNIL pages I opened uses the term.
verdicts.why: The conclusion is consistent with every source I opened — neither CNIL page mentions double opt-in, and no text I read imposes it. But the supporting quote is not on the cited page. I checked the opt-in/opt-out URL twice: it contains neither "libre, spécifique, éclairé et univoque" nor "case à cocher" nor "pré-cochée". The first half of the quote is real and sits on CNIL's consent definition page ("Il doit être libre, spécifique, éclairé et univoque."); the checkbox half appears elsewhere again. So the memo's quote is stitched from at least two other pages and attributed to a third that carries neither. That is the one citation in this set that would not survive anyone opening the link, and it sits on the claim already marked medium confidence.
verdicts.correction: Cite the consent formula to https://www.cnil.fr/fr/definition/consentement-rgpd and drop the composite quote. The recommendation of double opt-in on evidentiary grounds stands.

verdicts.claim: CNIL's opt-in/opt-out explainer independently confirms the non-commercial carve-out by listing "prospection caritative" on the opt-out side.
verdicts.why: The page does list prospection caritative on the opt-out side, alongside postal advertising, electronic advertising for similar products or services, and B2B. The source_quote is a paraphrase written as a quotation — the page's own wording runs "la publicité adressée par voie postale ainsi que la publicité par voie électronique pour des produits ou services similaires" and "la prospection à destination de professionnels (B to B)", as separate items. Substance holds, wording does not, so do not paste that sentence anywhere as a quote. One live item spotted on the same page and absent from the memo: the loi du 30 juin 2025 made telephone démarchage opt-in from 11 août 2026. It does not touch email, but if he ever collects phone numbers the régime there is now the strict one.
verdicts.correction: Quote the page's actual four items, or present the sentence as a summary rather than a quotation.

verdicts.claim: (a) A domiciliation commerciale is an administrative/legal address supplied by an approved business centre; having an address is compulsory for any registered business.
verdicts.why: F37412 ("Domicilier une société et son activité", Vérifié le 15 septembre 2025) carries all three: domiciliation obligatoire, agrément préfectoral, contract of 3 mois minimum. The individual-business page checks out too — F2160, "Domicilier son entreprise individuelle et son activité", Vérifié le 02 juillet 2026, domiciliation described as obligatoire and "un préalable indispensable à la création, avant l'immatriculation". One thing the memo leaves out that matters for his decision: the same page says he may domicile at his own home — "Vous pouvez domicilier votre entreprise à votre adresse personnelle d'habitation" — with no time limit, and may request non-diffusion of that personal address. So a paid provider is the answer to publication on the website, not a legal requirement in itself.

verdicts.claim: (a) SeDomicilier, article dated 8 July 2026: 20 €/month HT with no commitment (16 € promo), down to 14 €/month HT on a 3-year commitment (11 € promo).
verdicts.why: The date (8 July 2026), the four figures (20 / 16 / 14 / 11) and the legal-form line all check out — the page's own wording is "Le tarif ne dépend pas de la forme juridique", slightly shorter than the memo's rendering. The HT framing is the problem: the page does not state HT or TTC anywhere. The memo asserts "All figures excl. VAT" as fact. At 20% that turns 20 €/month into 24 €, and 14 € into 16.80 € — a real gap on a number he is about to budget against. Vendor-published price list either way.
verdicts.correction: Say the page does not state whether the figures are HT or TTC, and confirm with the provider before budgeting.

verdicts.claim: (a) LegalPlace, guide 'Dernière mise à jour le 18/05/2026': 17 € HT/month for a micro-entreprise or SCI, 25 € HT/month for a SARL/EURL/SAS/SASU, address in Paris 2e.
verdicts.why: The date, both prices and the HT marking are verbatim on the page, and the market range is given as "entre 10 € et 70 € HT par mois" — the memo is right to call that vendor editorial rather than a survey. The Paris 2e detail is not on this page; it came from somewhere else and is presented as though it were part of the cited quote. Minor, but it is the kind of detail he would repeat to a provider.
verdicts.correction: Drop 'address in Paris 2e' or source it separately.

verdicts.claim: (a) Third named provider, Kandbaz: association address advertised at under 20 €/month, with a 1 €/month 3-month promo.
verdicts.why: Both figures are on the page — "moins de 20 €/mois" in the FAQ answering the cost of domiciling an association, and "Domiciliation dès 1€/mois pendant 3 mois avec le code KAND1EU". Two corrections. The page does carry a visible date, "Actualisé le 11 février 2026", so the memo's note that it is dated only by the fetch is wrong. And the 1 € promo sits at the top of the page as a general site-wide offer, not an association-specific one — only the under-20 € figure is association-specific. The memo has it the other way round.
verdicts.correction: Page is dated 11 February 2026; the 1 €/month promo is site-wide, not association-specific.

audits.overall:
Every URL opened; every source exists. The legal spine is sound: article 1-1 LCEN really did replace article 6-III on 23 May 2024, L34-5's definition of prospection directe really is commercial by construction, CNIL really does run a non-commercial carve-out on opt-out, and no French text I opened puts a postal address inside a message. The Brevo wall really is a CAN-SPAM artefact.

Four things would expose him if he acted on this as written.

The anonymity option is not available to him yet. Article 1-1 II requires him to have given the host "les éléments d'identification personnelle mentionnés au I" — and section I for a personne physique is literally nom, prénoms, domicile et numéro de téléphone. A GitHub account holds a username and an email. Until he actually supplies those four items and keeps proof, the paragraph the memo relies on has no condition satisfied. This is the single most load-bearing error in the set.

"L34-5 is not triggered" is a reading, not a finding. The definition catches promotion "directement ou indirectement" of the goods of a person who sells — it does not require the seller to be the sender. A culinary letter naming producers, wines or shops is reachable on the text alone, and I found no decision holding otherwise. Enforcement also runs through the DGCCRF, not only the CNIL, so CNIL's non-commercial doctrine is not a defence there. And his own freemium plan retires the premise within months.

One citation would not survive a click. The double-opt-in claim's quote is not on the page it cites — that page contains neither "libre, spécifique, éclairé et univoque" nor "case à cocher" nor "pré-cochée". The formula is real but lives on CNIL's consent definition page; the quote as given is stitched from two other pages. The conclusion is fine; the evidence is not.

The nine-item privacy notice is ten for him. CNIL lists the droit de retrait du consentement among the mentions required "selon les cas", and the memo's own previous claim puts him on consent. Also: article 19 LCEN is cited at a version that expires 1 January 2027, and the memo omits the free RNE non-diffusion request, which is the cheap half of the address-privacy fix.

The domiciliation prices are accurate with two exceptions — SeDomicilier's page never says HT (the memo asserts it; at 20% that is 20 € becoming 24 €), and the Kandbaz page is dated 11 February 2026, contradicting the memo's note that it carries no date.

verdicts.claim: (b) No. A commercial domiciliation contract is sold to a business — existing or in the course of registration — not to a private individual with no entity and no project.
verdicts.why: The quoted sentence is on the Kandbaz page verbatim (dated 19 November 2025): 'Avant la signature d'un contrat de domiciliation, le domiciliataire doit : identifier le client (entreprise) et, le cas échéant, le bénéficiaire effectif.' But that sentence proves an anti-money-laundering identification duty, not a rule about who may buy. The real anchor is the code de commerce itself: the sub-section governing the regulated activity is titled 'Domiciliation des personnes immatriculées' (L123-10 to L123-11-8), and L123-11-3 subjects domiciliataires to prior agrément. So the claim holds for the regulated business-address product. It does not hold as a general statement about domiciliation companies: the SeDomicilier page cited under claim (b) below states the opposite for the unregulated mail product — 'les services de domiciliation ne sont pas réservés aux entreprises'.
verdicts.correction: Keep the conclusion, change the citation: anchor it on the code de commerce sub-section 'Domiciliation des personnes immatriculées' (L123-10 à L123-11-8) rather than on an AML page, and say 'the regulated business-address contract' rather than 'a commercial domiciliation contract', since a separate unregulated mail-address product is sold to individuals.

verdicts.claim: (b) You can sign before the entity exists: the attestation/contrat de domiciliation is what lets you register, and it may carry the mention 'en cours d'immatriculation' instead of a SIREN.
verdicts.why: The phrase is on the LegalPlace guide verbatim, inside the list of what the attestation must contain: 'Le numéro SIREN (ou la mention « en cours d'immatriculation » si l'entreprise n'est pas encore créée).' Page last updated 13/04/2026 as stated. Two caveats: LegalPlace is a commercial guide, not a legal source, and the page nowhere states directly that the contract may be signed pre-incorporation — that follows from the SIREN placeholder and from the attestation being the justificatif de jouissance filed at the guichet unique, which is sound but is an inference. The practical consequence stated for him is right and is the part that matters: he cannot usefully buy the address before deciding to create the entity.

verdicts.claim: (b) What a private individual can buy instead is a mail box (domiciliation postale). It is explicitly not a proof of residence and is not a personal address.
verdicts.why: The substance is supported, but the cited page contradicts the reasoning given for it on one material point. The page's actual sentence is 'you cannot use the address of your domiciliation box as a proof of address' — the quoted wording is a paraphrase, not verbatim. And the detail says SeDomicilier 'sells the service to individuals'; the page says the reverse in terms: 'SeDomicilier ne propose pas de service de domiciliation pour les particuliers.' What the page does establish is the general point — 'les services de domiciliation ne sont pas réservés aux entreprises… les particuliers peuvent également bénéficier de ces services' — while noting not all providers offer it. Separately, the 'not a justificatif de domicile' limitation is the wrong test for his actual use: GDPR and LCEN ask for a contact address for the publisher, not for proof of where he sleeps, so a box address failing as a justificatif does not by itself disqualify it from a newsletter footer.
verdicts.correction: Replace the SeDomicilier attribution — it does not sell to individuals, it says the market does. Use the page for the general proposition only, and drop the 'not a proof of residence' point from the newsletter analysis, where it is not the applicable test.

verdicts.claim: (c) Alternative — attestation d'hébergement from a third party (school, employer, parent). Mechanically possible: a host signs an attestation authorising the business address at their premises.
verdicts.why: The LegalPlace sentence exists — 'Une attestation d'hébergement signée par la personne qui vous héberge, indiquant qu'elle vous autorise à domicilier votre entreprise à son adresse' — but the claim's English rendering is a translation, not a quote. The Service-Public corroboration asserted in the detail is not there: I searched the cited EI page (F2160) for 'attestation d'hébergement', 'hébergé', 'justificatif de domicile' and '3 mois' and found none, and the page's enumeration of domiciliation options is own home, dedicated premises, société de domiciliation agréée, coworking, pépinière — the third-party-host route is absent. So the route rests on one commercial guide while the government page that lists the options omits it. One further risk the claim does not name: hosting someone else's business address as an activity is precisely what L123-11-3 subjects to agrément, so this is safe as free family hosting and gets legally awkward the moment it looks like a service.
verdicts.correction: Drop the Service-Public attribution (the '3-month justificatif in the host's name' detail is not on F2160) and downgrade the route from 'alternative on the table' to 'stated by a commercial guide, not by the official enumeration'.

verdicts.claim: (c) Alternative — La Poste boîte postale (Flexigo). Rentable by individuals, annual or seasonal, but you must prove a home address to get one, and the page publishes no price.
verdicts.why: All four checkable facts are on the page: the definition quote verbatim ('Une boîte postale constitue un espace de stockage personnel situé dans un bureau de Poste.'), the requirement to 'présenter une pièce d'identité valide et justifier de votre domicile', the annual/seasonal choice with automatic renewal 'chaque premier janvier', the Flexigo branding, and no tariff anywhere on the page. Two sourcing notes: the association/boîte-postale point attributed to Kandbaz is real but sits on a different Kandbaz page (domiciliation-association), not on either page cited in this claim set; and nothing on the La Poste page addresses whether a BP may be printed as a published contact address, so that remains open. For him the binding constraint is the one the claim already names: a BP requires a home address to obtain, so it conceals his address rather than replacing it.

verdicts.claim: (c) Alternative — coworking space or pépinière d'entreprises, listed by Service-Public as valid domiciliation for an EI/micro-entreprise.
verdicts.why: F2160 (verified 2 July 2026) carries the quoted sentence verbatim — 'La domiciliation de votre entreprise (EI… ou micro-entreprise) est obligatoire.' — and lists both coworking and pépinière among the options, with the pépinière limits as stated: registered within 6 months maximum, hosting capped at 48 months. The claim's own qualifier is the operative one: both presuppose an entity, so neither is available to him today.

verdicts.claim: (c) INSEE/INPI rule — whatever address an entrepreneur declares goes into Sirene and the Registre national des entreprises, and is republished on the public Annuaire des entreprises unless he opposes.
verdicts.why: The INSEE page dated 02/12/2025 carries 'Les autres informations concernant l'unité légale restent diffusées' verbatim, cites both article R123-232-1 of the code de commerce and article 21 GDPR, and lists for catégorie juridique 1000 exactly the withheld fields stated: name, first names, pseudonym, enseigne and nom commercial, exact address within the commune, and geolocation variables.

verdicts.claim: (d) An association loi 1901 does give a publishable address — but the declaration publishes that address in the Journal officiel, so it solves nothing if the siège is his home.
verdicts.why: The four-field JOAFE list is on the associations.gouv.fr page verbatim — 'Date de la déclaration en préfecture, Titre de l'association, Objet, Adresse du siège de l'association' — so the siège address is published. The conclusion follows: the association only helps if the siège is somewhere other than his flat.

verdicts.claim: (d) Cost to create: zero. Declaration and Journal officiel publication have both been free since 2019.
verdicts.why: The page states 'Cette démarche est gratuite depuis 2019', delivers the récépissé 'dans les 5 jours suivant la remise du dossier complet', and publishes extracts 'le mardi de chaque semaine'. The quoted 'free since 2019' is an English rendering of the French sentence, not a verbatim quote.

verdicts.claim: (d) The declaration also files the administrators' names, professions, addresses and nationality with the préfecture — so his home address reaches the administration even when it is not the siège.
verdicts.why: The page carries the requirement verbatim in French: 'Noms, professions, domicile et nationalité des personnes qui à un titre quelconque sont chargées de son administration.' The claim's English is a translation. The inference that these fields are filed rather than published is sound, since the JOAFE announcement is the four fields verified above and does not include them; the page itself does not state it either way, which the claim's own caveat already concedes.

verdicts.claim: (d) What the association buys him: legal personality — a bank account, contracts, subsidies — i.e. a legal person that can be the newsletter's data controller instead of him personally.
verdicts.why: The page states 'Toute association dite loi 1901 qui veut obtenir la capacité juridique doit d'abord effectuer une déclaration préalable', so declaration is what confers capacity. The data-controller consequence is a correct legal inference, not text on the page. Worth naming for him: the association changes who the controller is, not who is identifiable — he is still declared by name and domicile as an administrator, and the siège address is still published, so it is an address fix only when the siège sits somewhere other than his flat.

verdicts.claim: (d) Siège at his own home is lawful — a lease cannot forbid it — but that is exactly the address the Journal officiel would publish.
verdicts.why: Both quotes are on the page (dated 17 June 2025): 'Un contrat de location ne peut pas interdire à un locataire l'exercice d'une activité associative', and for an owner outside copropriété 'vous êtes libre de domicilier le siège social de votre association à votre domicile. Vous n'avez pas besoin d'autorisation'. The claim omits one condition the page attaches to the tenant case: 'le logement doit bien rester votre lieu d'habitation. Il ne peut pas devenir le lieu de l'activité effective de l'association par la transformation du logement en bureau.' Harmless for a newsletter, but it is the condition, and it should travel with the rule.
verdicts.correction: Add the tenant condition: the home must remain his actual residence and cannot become the association's operating premises.

verdicts.claim: (e) Yes — a micro-entreprise declared at home publishes that home address by default, and no, it is not unavoidable: an online opposition makes only the commune public.
verdicts.why: F2160 (verified 2 July 2026) carries 'Seule la commune de résidence sera rendue publique sur le Registre national des entreprises (RNE)' verbatim and links the online service; the FranceConnect login, the need for the SIREN, and the 48-hour effect are corroborated at statut-diffusion-sirene.insee.fr and the INSEE page. One sequencing trap the claim does not name: the opposition needs a SIREN, so it can only be filed after registration — his address is diffusible for the gap between immatriculation and the change taking effect, and anything scraped by third-party company-data sites during that window is outside INSEE's reach.
verdicts.correction: Add the timing caveat — the masking is retrospective on the registers but not on copies already taken, so the opposition should be filed the same day the SIREN arrives.

verdicts.claim: (e) Separate, newer protection: décret n° 2025-840 du 22 août 2025 lets company officers hide their personal address on the RCS, and the INPI states the RNE does not diffuse representatives' personal addresses.
verdicts.why: The INPI page (published 27 August 2025) carries 'Le RNE ne diffuse pas les adresses personnelles des représentants d'entreprises.' verbatim and links the décret. The décret's scope matches the claim's warning: it covers dirigeants and associés indéfiniment responsables of legal persons mentioned at article R123-54, filing through the INPI guichet unique, with the greffier acting within five working days, in force 25 August 2025. It does not reach an entrepreneur individuel, so the claim's refusal to conflate the two tracks is correct.

verdicts.claim: (e) TRAP: registering a micro-entreprise puts his address back on the site itself. LCEN mentions légales for an entrepreneur individuel's website require 'votre nom, prénom et adresse'.
verdicts.why: F31228 (vérifié le 31 juillet 2023) says exactly 'votre nom, prénom et adresse. Si vous êtes entrepreneur individuel (y compris, micro-entrepreneur), vos nom et prénom sont accompagnés de la mention entrepreneur individuel ou des initiales EI', with the penalty stated as one year and 75 000 €. If anything the claim understates the exposure twice over: F31228 also requires the RCS number, a phone number, an email and the host's identity, and the statute behind it (LCEN article 6, III-1) says 'domicile' for a natural person, not 'an address' — which is why a domiciliation address here is market practice rather than a textually watertight cure.
verdicts.correction: State the statutory word: LCEN III-1 requires the natural person's 'domicile', so a domiciliation address is the accepted practice, not a guaranteed substitute — and the mentions légales also drag in his phone number and RCS/SIREN, not just an address.

verdicts.claim: Today, with no entity, he is not required to publish any address: a non-professional publisher may identify their host instead of themselves.
verdicts.why: The CNIL quote is verbatim ('Le blogueur doit s'identifier ou indiquer le nom de son hébergeur'), but the CNIL page is from 12 June 2009 and states the rule without its conditions. The statute is LCEN article 6, III-2: a non-professional natural person may keep anonymity by publishing 'le nom, la dénomination ou la raison sociale et l'adresse du fournisseur de services d'hébergement', on condition that he has communicated his own identifying elements to that host, which is then bound by professional secrecy. So an address must appear on the page — the host's — and 'not required to publish any address' is wrong as written. His current footer, described as naming GitHub Pages with no address, is therefore incomplete under the very provision relied on.
verdicts.correction: Restate as: he need not publish his own address, but he must publish the host's name and postal address and must be identifiable to the host. Add GitHub's published postal address to the footer; the exemption also lapses the day the site is published 'à titre professionnel'.

verdicts.claim: GDPR-side, the controller's 'coordonnées' in a collection notice need not be postal — the CNIL's own model leaves the channel open.
verdicts.why: Both elements are on the CNIL page dated 26 juillet 2019 verbatim: the placeholder '[adresse électronique, postale, coordonnées téléphoniques, etc.]' and the warning 'Il s'agit d'une illustration, qu'il vous appartient d'adapter ou de compléter, et non d'un modèle de mention valable dans toutes les hypothèses.' The conclusion holds for him and is reinforced by the definition the commercial-email regime turns on: article L34-5 CPCE bites on 'prospection directe', defined as a message promoting goods, services, or the image of a person selling goods or providing services — which a free newsletter with nothing for sale is not. Brevo's postal-address demand is its own policy, inherited from US anti-spam law, not French or EU law applied to him.

verdicts.claim: Side finding — copius.fr itself is not leaking his address: AFNIC hides natural-person holders' data from the public Whois by default.
verdicts.why: The AFNIC expert paper dated 22 April 2021 states that 'the personal data of domain name holders who are natural persons are not published in the directory service available to the general public', and that selecting 'natural person' at registration protects the holder's contact details 'by default'. The recommended check on the OVH record is the right one, since the protection follows that flag. One limit worth stating: this is confidentiality from the public Whois, not secrecy — AFNIC still discloses to qualified requesters through its own procedure.

audits.overall:
Fifteen of seventeen claims survive re-opening the sources; two are overstated and one carries a material error in its supporting reasoning. No claim commits the professionnel/particulier conflation the audit was watching for — the set is careful about it, and claim (e) on the décret of 22 August 2025 explicitly refuses to conflate the dirigeant track with the entrepreneur individuel track, correctly.

The two findings that change what he should do:

First, the claim that he need publish no address today is wrong as written, and it is wrong in the direction that exposes him. LCEN article 6, III-2 lets a non-professional natural person stay anonymous only by publishing the host's name AND postal address, and only if he has given his own identifying details to that host. His described footer — GitHub Pages named, no address — does not satisfy the provision he is relying on. That is a ten-minute fix, and it is the only thing on this list he needs to do now.

Second, the attestation d'hébergement route is presented as an alternative on the table on the strength of a Service-Public corroboration that is not there. I searched the cited EI page (F2160) for 'attestation d'hébergement', 'hébergé', 'justificatif de domicile' and '3 mois': none appear, and the page's enumeration of domiciliation options — own home, dedicated premises, société de domiciliation agréée, coworking, pépinière — omits the third-party-host route entirely. It rests on one commercial guide.

The error of reasoning: the claim about mail boxes says SeDomicilier 'sells the service to individuals'. The page says 'SeDomicilier ne propose pas de service de domiciliation pour les particuliers.' The general proposition it does support — domiciliation services are not reserved to businesses — survives; the attribution does not. And the 'not a justificatif de domicile' limitation is the wrong test for the newsletter anyway: what a footer needs is a contact address for the publisher, not proof of residence.

One structural note on the whole set. Every route costing money or creating an entity is a consequence of registering, not of writing a newsletter. As things stand — private individual, nothing for sale, free newsletter — article L34-5 CPCE does not reach him (it turns on promoting goods, services, or the image of a seller), the CNIL's own template leaves the controller's coordonnées to any channel, and LCEN lets him hide behind his host. The postal address Brevo demanded is Brevo's policy, inherited from US anti-spam law. The cheapest correct answer may be a different ESP, not an address, an association, or a micro-entreprise — and claim (e)'s trap is the reason to be slow about the last of those: the day he registers, the mentions légales put his name, his 'domicile' as the statute words it, his phone number and his SIREN back on the page, and INSEE non-diffusion does nothing about that.
